top.line: A coding standard is a behaviour policy: write it as intent, see what holds each rule, and map it across teams with a graph.
top.para: Coding standards describe how agents behave when they write code. Our own, measured by coding.sgit.ai, are 31 rules kept by habit with no passing CI guard: a mandate with no barrier. Fractal semantic graphs connect intent, stories, features, classes and methods, so common intents can keep teams and languages in step, and language models make the mappings affordable.

in-short.line: A standard is a policy; intent is the power; ours are measured; the gap shows; graphs connect layers; common intents align teams.

idea.line: A data policy and a coding standard both describe behaviour, and both work because they describe intent.
idea.para: The intent survives a change of tool; a linter flag is one way of keeping it.

ours.line: coding.sgit.ai measured our standards: 31 rules, no linters, four guards that encode incidents, no rule with a passing guard.
ours.para: The rules are mostly kept by habit; read as a policy, the barrier column shows what holds each one.

graph.line: The sgit CLI graph reads one commit upwards to nine commands and six stories.
graph.para: Ten house rules run as graph queries: a rule is a shape, a violation a node where it is missing.

common.line: A cart feature across back end, front end and data tier can carry one set of common intents into each language.
common.para: Each language keeps an intent its own way; the graph shows the whole change serves it, and where no barrier holds yet.

models.line: Models make the mappings cheap; users, experts and tests confirm them.
models.para: Proposals stay marked until confirmed; corrections are commits to the graph files.

limits.line: The cart example is invented; the figures are coding.sgit.ai's and the worked example's.
limits.para: Mapping across many languages and teams is a proposal.

sources.line: A conversation on 12 November, coding.sgit.ai, and earlier newsroom articles.
